title: Design a Distributed Key-Value Store
tagline: Build a Dynamo-style store that stays up when machines die and grows by adding nodes.

statement.prompt: Design a **distributed key-value store** like DynamoDB or Cassandra. Clients `put` and `get` values by key. The data is too big and too busy for one machine.
context: You are in a 45-minute interview. This is a classic deep-dive question about partitioning, replication and consistency.
The store is used by many teams for sessions, carts and profiles.
Latency should be a few milliseconds even at huge scale.
given: About **100 TB** of data before replication.
Millions of operations per second across the cluster.
Machines fail every day. The service must not.
Values are small (a few KB), keys are strings.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are partitioning with consistent hashing, replication with quorums, and handling failures and conflicts.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

scope_in: put, get and delete by key
The storage engine on each node
great: Uses **consistent hashing with virtual nodes**, not hash mod N.
Explains **N, W, R** and why R + W > N matters.
Describes **hinted handoff, read repair and anti-entropy** for repair.
Handles **conflicting writes** and names the CAP choice.

concepts.def: Place nodes and keys on a ring; a key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding a node moves only a small share of keys.
One machine appears at many points on the ring so load is even.
The number of replicas that must respond. Write quorum W and read quorum R with R + W > N give fresh reads.
A version counter per replica used to tell whether two writes are ordered or concurrent.
Nodes exchange state with random peers so information spreads without a master.
Write to a log and memtable, flush sorted files, merge in the background. Very fast writes.
A compact structure that says 'definitely not here' or 'maybe here'.

numbers: N=3, W=2, R=2 is the usual balanced setting
Replication multiplies storage: **100 TB x 3 = 300 TB**
Consistent hashing moves only about **1/N** of keys when a node joins

takeaways: Partition with **consistent hashing and virtual nodes**; replicate each key to **N=3** nodes in different failure domains.
Use **quorums**: R + W > N for fresh reads, lower values for speed.
Repair with **hinted handoff, read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy**; detect failure with **gossip**.
State the choice: **AP with tunable consistency**, and **LSM storage** on each node.

tradeoffs.gain: Always answers, even in a partition

repair.label:
Hinted handoff
read repair
Merkle trees

steps.title: What is the API?
steps.prompt: A key-value store. Which operations belong in scope?
steps.hint: What is the smallest useful contract?
steps.explain: A KV store promises **simple, fast access by key** at any scale. Anything that needs scanning or joining belongs elsewhere.

notes: API: put, get, delete; scale by adding nodes; tunable consistency

options.text: Tunable consistency per request
options.why: Lets callers pick speed or freshness.

options.text: Scale by adding nodes, without downtime
options.why: Why we build it distributed.

options.text: `delete(key)`
options.why: Remove (usually a tombstone marker).

options.text: `put(key, value)`
options.why: Write.

options.text: Joins and SQL queries across keys
options.why: That is a relational database, not a key-value store.

options.text: Full-text search over values
options.why: A different system.

options.text: `get(key)`
options.why: Read.

steps.title: What qualities drive the design?
steps.hint: Which two of CAP will you favour?
steps.explain: We are building an **AP, horizontally scalable** store. Say it: *"I choose availability over strict consistency during partitions."*

notes: Qualities: highly available, horizontally scalable, low latency, eventually consistent by default

options.text: Horizontal scalability to many TB and millions of ops/s
options.why: Add machines, not a bigger machine.

options.text: Low latency (single-digit milliseconds)
options.why: Direct key access, no scans.

options.text: Serializable multi-key transactions
options.why: Would need heavy coordination. Out of scope.

options.text: High availability: reads and writes keep working when nodes fail
options.why: A core selling point of Dynamo-style stores.

options.text: Eventual consistency by default, stronger on request
options.why: AP in CAP terms with a dial.

steps.title: How many nodes?
steps.prompt: You must store **100 TB** (before replication) and keep **3 copies** of each item. Each node holds **10 TB**. How many **nodes** are needed (ignore spare capacity)?
steps.explain: **About 30 nodes minimum, 40+ in practice.** Notice how replication multiplies storage by 3, so replication factor is a real cost decision.

notes: Capacity: 100 TB x 3 replicas = 300 TB, about 30-40 nodes of 10 TB

work: 100 TB x 3 copies = **300 TB** on disk
Add headroom (compaction needs free space, nodes fail) so plan for **40 or more**

steps.title: How do we place keys?
steps.prompt: Which scheme decides which node holds a key, so that adding a node moves little data?
steps.hint: What happens to `% N` when N changes?
steps.explain: **Consistent hashing + virtual nodes** gives even spread and smooth growth. This idea appears in Dynamo, Cassandra and many caches.

notes: Partitioning: consistent hashing ring with virtual nodes

steps.followup: Why use hundreds of virtual nodes per machine rather than one?

options.text: Consistent hashing on a ring, with many virtual nodes per machine
options.why: Adding a node takes a slice from many neighbours; only about 1/N of keys move.

options.text: `hash(key) % number_of_nodes`
options.why: Change N and almost every key maps to a different node: a mass reshuffle.

options.text: A central table mapping every key to a node
options.why: A bottleneck and single point of failure for 10 billion keys.

options.text: Range partitioning by first letter of the key
options.why: Hot ranges (many keys start with `a`) and uneven load.

steps.title: How many copies and where?
steps.prompt: A node can die at any time and so can a whole rack or zone. How do you replicate?
steps.explain: **N=3, in different failure domains.** Spread copies so that no single event can take out every replica.

notes: Replication: N=3 on distinct nodes in different racks/zones

options.text: Store each key on the next N=3 distinct nodes clockwise, placed in different racks or zones
options.why: Survives a node, a rack or a zone loss.

options.text: Three copies, but all on the same rack
options.why: One power failure loses all three.

options.text: Copy everything to every node
options.why: Storage and write cost explode.

options.text: Keep one copy and rely on backups
options.why: Restoring takes hours and loses recent writes.

steps.title: Quorum maths
steps.prompt: With **N = 3** replicas and a write quorum **W = 2**, what is the smallest read quorum **R** that guarantees a read sees the latest write (R + W > N)?
steps.hint: Two sets overlap if their sizes add to more than the total.
steps.explain: **N=3, W=2, R=2** is the common balanced setting. **W=1, R=1** is the fastest and weakest. **W=3** survives no failures on writes. Quorums give you the *dial* between speed and freshness.

notes: Quorum: N=3, W=2, R=2 (R + W > N) for strongly fresh reads; W=1/R=1 for speed

steps.followup: What happens to availability if you set W=3?
work: With W=2, R=2: any 2 replicas read must overlap with the 2 that acknowledged the write

steps.title: Two writers, same key
steps.prompt: Two clients write the same key at the same moment via different coordinators, so replicas disagree. What do you do?
steps.explain: **Last-write-wins** (timestamps) is simple but can lose a write if clocks differ. **Vector clocks** detect concurrency so the application can merge, like merging shopping carts.

notes: Conflicts: vector clocks to detect, app-level merge or last-write-wins

options.text: Lock the key across the whole cluster for every write
options.why: Kills availability and latency.

options.text: Always keep the larger value
options.why: Arbitrary and loses information.

options.text: Pretend it cannot happen
options.why: It will, in a partition.

options.text: Detect with version vectors / vector clocks, and either merge in the app or fall back to last-write-wins for simple data
options.why: You know the versions are concurrent, not just 'newer'.

steps.title: A node is down during a write
steps.prompt: N=3, W=2. One replica is unreachable. Order what happens.
steps.explain: Three layers of repair: **hinted handoff** (short outages), **read repair** (when a read sees a stale copy), **anti-entropy with Merkle trees** (long outages). No single repair is enough.

notes: Repair: hinted handoff, read repair, Merkle-tree anti-entropy

items.text: The coordinator sends the write to all three replicas
Two replicas acknowledge; the third times out
The coordinator tells the client success and stores a hint for the down node on another node (hinted handoff)
When the down node returns, the hint is replayed to it
items.why: Brings it back up to date.

items.text: Merkle-tree comparison (anti-entropy) repairs any remaining differences in the background
items.why: A safety net for longer outages.

steps.title: Detecting failure
steps.prompt: No master node. How do nodes know who is alive?
steps.hint: How can many nodes agree without a boss?
steps.explain: Decentralised **gossip + heartbeats** keeps the cluster master-less. Mention the **phi accrual** detector if you know it.

notes: Membership: gossip protocol and heartbeat failure detection, seed nodes to join

options.text: One master node that pings everyone
options.why: The master becomes a single point of failure.

options.text: Failure suspicion based on missed heartbeats, with a timeout threshold
options.why: Avoids marking a slow node dead too early.

options.text: Clients decide by guessing
options.why: No shared truth.

options.text: Seed nodes to bootstrap new members
options.why: A new node needs someone to contact first.

options.text: **Gossip**: every second each node swaps its view of the cluster with a few random peers
options.why: Information spreads like a rumour, no single point of failure.

steps.title: On one node
steps.prompt: How does a single node store and find data quickly?
steps.hint: Write fast to a log, organise later.
steps.explain: This is an **LSM tree**. Writes are sequential and fast; reads check memory first, then files, with Bloom filters keeping that cheap.

notes: Node storage: commit log + memtable + SSTables + Bloom filters + compaction (LSM tree)

options.text: Keep recent writes in an in-memory **memtable**
options.why: Fast reads and batching.

options.text: Append every write to a **commit log** for durability
options.why: Sequential writes are fast and survive a crash.

options.text: Rewrite the whole data file for every put
options.why: Painfully slow.

options.text: Flush the memtable as immutable sorted files (**SSTables**) and compact them in the background
options.why: The LSM-tree design: fast writes, organised reads.

options.text: Use **Bloom filters** to skip files that cannot contain the key
options.why: Avoids reading many files for a missing key.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: which side of CAP did you pick, and what does it cost?
steps.hint: What can a reader see that is not the latest?
steps.explain: The best answers say **both** what the system is good for and what it is wrong for.

notes: Trade-offs: AP with tunable quorums; costs stale reads and conflict handling

steps.model: I chose **availability and partition tolerance (AP)**: the store keeps accepting reads and writes during a partition and repairs differences later. The cost is **eventual consistency**: a read might briefly return old data, and concurrent writes need conflict handling. Quorums let callers dial toward stronger consistency (R + W > N) at the cost of latency and availability. For use cases like bank balances I would pick a CP system instead.
points: Chose AP and said what that means
Said when a CP store is the better choice
